query: We are investigating the atomic-scale thermal behavior of AuCoCuNiPt high-entropy alloy (HENA) nanoparticles synthesized via pulsed laser deposition on a silicon nitride membrane. The prevailing hypothesis is that high entropy and sluggish diffusion stabilize the FCC structure against coalescence and segregation. However, in situ heating experiments reveal a progressive loss of sub-5 nm particles and a widening of the size distribution, alongside a reshaping from elliptical to spherical geometries. Theoretical models based on Gibbs free energy often neglect surface energy terms critical for sub-10 nm systems. It has been observed that the FCC structure in these PLD-grown NPs may be governed by kinetic effects rather than entropy. Propose a mechanism explaining why atomic diffusion is surprisingly active in this quinary system, leading to the segregation of specific elements (like Au and Cu) to the surface and subsequent evaporation. Identify the critical temperature threshold where this mechanism becomes dominant, establish the boundary conditions regarding the initial nanoparticle shape (icosahedral vs. truncated octahedron), and formulate a falsification experiment involving simultaneous in situ STEM and atomistic simulations to test if surface energy gradients alone can explain the observed phase separation without invoking sluggish diffusion.

generation.hypothesis: In AuCoCuNiPt high-entropy alloy nanoparticles, atomic diffusion is driven by surface energy gradients rather than sluggish diffusion, leading to segregation of low-surface-energy elements (Au, Cu) to the surface and subsequent evaporation. This mechanism becomes dominant above a critical temperature threshold of ~450 K, where surface diffusion coefficients exceed bulk diffusion by orders of magnitude due to reduced coordination numbers. The initial nanoparticle shape (icosahedral vs. truncated octahedron) critically influences the segregation pathway: icosahedral particles exhibit faster surface diffusion due to higher surface curvature and defect density, accelerating segregation, while truncated octahedrons show slower kinetics due to lower surface energy anisotropy. Surface energy gradients alone can explain the observed phase separation without invoking sluggish diffusion.
generation.material_initial_state: AuCoCuNiPt high-entropy alloy nanoparticles (sub-5 nm) synthesized via pulsed laser deposition on silicon nitride membrane, initially exhibiting FCC structure with elliptical geometry and uniform elemental distribution.
generation.intervention: In situ heating from room temperature to 600 K under vacuum conditions, with simultaneous monitoring of particle size distribution, shape evolution, and elemental composition.
generation.conditions: Temperature range: 300–600 K; Pressure: <10^-6 Pa; Particle size: 2–8 nm; Initial shape: Icosahedral or truncated octahedron; Atmosphere: Ultra-high vacuum to prevent oxidation.
generation.structural_mediator: Surface energy gradients creating chemical potential differences that drive element-specific segregation, with Au and Cu preferentially migrating to the surface due to their lower surface energies compared to Co, Ni, and Pt.
generation.mechanism: Surface diffusion dominates over bulk diffusion at elevated temperatures due to reduced activation energy barriers. Low-surface-energy elements (Au, Cu) segregate to the surface to minimize total surface energy, creating a concentration gradient that drives further segregation. Once segregated, these elements evaporate due to their high vapor pressures at elevated temperatures, leading to particle size reduction and widening of the size distribution. The FCC structure is maintained by kinetic trapping rather than thermodynamic stability from high entropy.
generation.predicted_outcome: Progressive loss of sub-5 nm particles, widening of size distribution, reshaping from elliptical to spherical geometries, and surface enrichment of Au and Cu followed by their evaporation. The critical temperature threshold of ~450 K marks the onset of dominant surface-driven segregation.
generation.baseline: Conventional high-entropy alloy theory predicts sluggish diffusion and entropy-stabilized FCC structure, expecting minimal segregation and coalescence up to higher temperatures.
generation.boundary: Mechanism applies to nanoparticles <10 nm where surface-to-volume ratio is high; fails for larger particles where bulk diffusion dominates. Shape dependence: Icosahedral particles show faster segregation than truncated octahedrons due to higher surface curvature and defect density.
generation.uncertainty: Exact critical temperature threshold may vary with specific composition ratios and initial particle morphology. Surface energy values for quinary systems may differ from binary/ternary approximations. Kinetic effects during PLD synthesis may introduce residual stresses affecting diffusion pathways.
generation.falsification_experiment: Conduct simultaneous in situ STEM and atomistic molecular dynamics simulations on AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles with controlled initial shapes (icosahedral vs. truncated octahedron). Vary temperature from 300–600 K while monitoring elemental segregation profiles and particle morphology. Compare experimental segregation rates with simulations that include only surface energy terms (excluding bulk diffusion contributions). If surface energy gradients alone reproduce the observed segregation and evaporation kinetics without invoking sluggish diffusion, the hypothesis is supported. If simulations require bulk diffusion terms to match experimental data, the hypothesis is falsified.
